hints: Think about which Lewis acid catalyst is used for bromination of an aromatic ring in the dark and how it polarises the Br-Br bond to release Br+.
walkthrough:
Recall what the catalyst must do**
You are brominating methylbenzene in the dark, so this is electrophilic substitution on the ring, not free radical substitution on the side chain. $\text{Br}_2$ alone is not electrophilic enough, so a Lewis acid is needed to pull electron density away and create a much stronger electrophile, $\text{Br}^{+}$.

Complete the ion pair**
The usual catalyst is $\text{AlBr}_3$ (or $\text{FeBr}_3$). It accepts $\text{Br}^{-}$ from $\text{Br}_2$ to give the electrophile and a large anion: $$\text{Br}_2 + \text{AlBr}_3 \rightarrow \text{Br}^{+} + \text{AlBr}_4^{-}$$

hints: Draw the three possible ring bromination products of methylbenzene and identify which positions are ortho, meta and para to the $\text{CH}_3$ group.
Recall whether a methyl group is activating and 2,4,6 directing or deactivating and 3,5 directing, and link this to which isomer is disfavoured.
walkthrough:
Picture the three isomers**
Methylbenzene can be brominated at positions 2 and 6 (ortho), position 4 (para) and positions 3 and 5 (meta) relative to the $\text{CH}_3$ group. The minor product is the one with $\text{Br}$ meta to $\text{CH}_3$, that is 3-bromo-methylbenzene (1-methyl-3-bromobenzene).

Link to the directing power of CH3**
Think of $\text{CH}_3$ as an electron donating group. It pushes electron density into the ring and stabilises the arenium intermediate best when attack occurs at the 2, 4 and 6 positions. In other words, $\text{CH}_3$ is 2,4,6 directing and activating. Attack at position 3 does not get this extra stabilisation, so the meta isomer forms much more slowly and in smallest amount.

Final answer: Structure: 3-bromo-methylbenzene, benzene ring with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{Br}$ in meta (1,3) positions.
The methyl group is activating and 2,4,6 (ortho and para) directing, so substitution at the 3 (meta) position is disfavoured and forms in smallest amount.

hints: Start from the pi electrons of the benzene ring attacking $\text{Br}^{+}$ and consider where the first curly arrow must begin and end.
Recall the structure of the positively charged arenium intermediate with Br attached and the positive charge delocalised around the ring.
Think about how aromaticity is restored by breaking a C-H bond and which small cation is expelled in the second step.
walkthrough:
Make the first bond to the electrophile**
Imagine the delocalised pi cloud of methylbenzene acting as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the $\text{Br}^{+}$ ion. This forms a new C-Br bond and breaks the aromaticity, giving a positively charged arenium (Wheland) intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the ring.

Draw the intermediate correctly**
Show a six membered ring with one saturated carbon bearing both Br and H (if ortho or para to $\text{CH}_3$), two double bonds remaining, and a + charge delocalised in the ring. The $\text{CH}_3$ group stays unchanged. This loss of aromaticity makes the intermediate high in energy.

Restore aromaticity to finish**
A base (often $\text{AlBr}_4^{-}$) removes the ring proton. Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bond at the same carbon that carries Br back into the hexagon to reform the pi system. The products are the bromo-methylbenzene (show the 2-bromo or 4-bromo isomer) plus $\text{H}^{+}$. That $\text{H}^{+}$ later reacts to give $\text{HBr}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from pi system inside hexagon to $\text{Br}^{+}$ to form arenium intermediate (cyclohexadienyl cation with Br attached, positive charge delocalised).
Curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to restore aromaticity, giving bromo-methylbenzene (2- or 4-isomer) + $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Compare hydrolysis of a C-Cl bond in a saturated alkyl chloride with that in chlorobenzene, and recall the colour of the silver halide precipitate that confirms chloride.
walkthrough:
Pick the reactive chloride**
You have an alkyl chloride and an aryl chloride. Only the halogenoalkane hydrolyses under warm aqueous conditions to release $\text{Cl}^{-}$. So chlorobutane is the one that reacts, and the free $\text{Cl}^{-}$ then gives a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3$ solution.
Final answer: Chlorobutane reacts, white precipitate (of $\text{AgCl}$) forms slowly.

hints: Write first the hydrolysis step where warm water replaces Cl by OH in chlorobutane and releases chloride ions and hydrogen ions.
Write second the precipitation step where the released chloride ion combines with silver ion from $\text{AgNO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Show where Cl- comes from**
Warm aqueous conditions slowly hydrolyse chlorobutane by nucleophilic substitution with water: $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH} + \text{H}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$$ This step is slow, which is why the precipitate appears slowly.

Show the test for Cl-**
Once $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is in solution it immediately precipitates with $\text{Ag}^{+}$: $$\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{AgCl}$$ The solid $\text{AgCl}$ is the observed white precipitate.

hints: Focus on the lone pairs on Cl in chlorobenzene and how they can interact with the delocalised pi system of the benzene ring.
Consider what this delocalisation does to the C-Cl bond order and strength, and why this prevents release of $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
See the overlap in chlorobenzene**
In chlorobenzene the Cl atom sits directly on the ring. One of its filled 3p lone pair orbitals can overlap sideways with the pi system of the ring, so the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.

Connect bonding to reactivity**
That overlap gives the C-Cl bond partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger than the pure C-Cl single bond in chlorobutane. Because much more energy is needed to break it, warm water cannot hydrolyse chlorobenzene, no $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is produced, and no precipitate forms with $\text{AgNO}_3$.

Final answer: In chlorobenzene a lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the benzene pi system.
This gives the C-Cl bond partial double bond character, making it stronger and harder to break, so no hydrolysis and no $\text{Cl}^{-}$ released.
